title: Implement git history parser for beads.jsonl
description:
# Git History Parser for beads.jsonl

## Context
This is the core extraction logic. We parse \`git log -p -- .beads/beads.jsonl\` to extract bead lifecycle events.

## Git Command
\`\`\`bash
git log -p --follow --format="%H|%aI|%an|%ae|%s" -- .beads/beads.jsonl
\`\`\`

## Parsing Algorithm
1. Run git log command
2. Parse output commit by commit
3. For each commit:
   a. Parse commit metadata (SHA, timestamp, author, message)
   b. Parse the diff section
   c. For each changed line in diff:
      - Parse old JSON (lines starting with -)
      - Parse new JSON (lines starting with +)
      - Detect what changed (new bead, status change, other)
      - Create BeadEvent records
4. Return chronologically sorted events

## Diff Parsing Details

### Detecting Bead Creation
\`\`\`diff
+{"id":"AUTH-123","title":"Fix login","status":"open",...}
\`\`\`
A line starting with \`+\` containing valid JSON = EventCreated

### Detecting Status Changes
\`\`\`diff
-{"id":"AUTH-123",...,"status":"open",...}
+{"id":"AUTH-123",...,"status":"in_progress",...}
\`\`\`
Same bead ID, different status = appropriate event type

## Edge Cases to Handle
1. Malformed JSON lines: Skip with warning
2. Multiple beads changed in one commit: Generate event for each
3. Empty commits: No events generated
4. Merge commits: Parse like regular commits

## Options Structure
\`\`\`go
type ExtractOptions struct {
    Since     time.Time  // Only commits after this time
    Until     time.Time  // Only commits before this time
    Limit     int        // Max commits to process
    BeadID    string     // Filter to single bead ID
}
\`\`\`

## File Location
\`pkg/correlation/extractor.go\`

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Correctly parses sample git log output
2. Handles all edge cases without panic
3. Returns chronologically sorted events
4. Supports filtering options
5. Unit tests with mock git output

title: Implement co-committed file extraction
description:
# Co-Committed File Extraction

## Context
This is the highest-confidence correlation method (95-99%). When a bead status changes and code files change in THE SAME COMMIT, that's a direct causal link.

## Why This Works
Developer workflow:
1. Write code to implement feature
2. Mark bead as closed
3. Commit both changes together

The code files in that commit ARE the implementation of the bead.

## Git Command
\`\`\`bash
git show --name-status --format="" <sha>
\`\`\`

Output:
\`\`\`
M       pkg/auth/login.go
M       pkg/auth/session.go
M       .beads/beads.jsonl
\`\`\`

## Algorithm
1. For each BeadEvent with status change (claimed/closed)
2. Run \`git show --name-status\` for that commit
3. Filter OUT bead files (.beads/*)
4. Return code files only as CorrelatedCommit records

## What Counts as "Code Files"?
Include: .go, .py, .js, .ts, .rs, .java, .yaml, .json, .md
Exclude: .beads/*, .bv/*, .git/*, node_modules/, vendor/

## Getting Line Stats
\`\`\`bash
git show --numstat --format="" <sha>
\`\`\`

## Confidence Scoring
Base: 0.95

Adjustments:
- Commit message mentions bead ID: +0.04 → 0.99
- >20 files changed (shotgun commit): -0.10 → 0.85
- Only test files changed: -0.05 → 0.90

## File Location
\`pkg/correlation/cocommit.go\`

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Correctly extracts co-committed files for any commit
2. Filters out bead files and non-code files
3. Includes insertion/deletion stats
4. Applies confidence adjustments correctly
5. Handles commits with no code files gracefully

title: [EPIC] Cass Integration - Coding Session Correlation
description:
# Epic: Cass Integration - Coding Session Correlation

## Vision
Surface relevant AI coding sessions from cass (Coding Agent Session Search) alongside beads, enabling users to see "how was this issue solved?" with one keypress. This bridges the gap between issue tracking (beads) and work history (cass sessions).

## Background

### What is cass?
cass (https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/coding_agent_session_search) indexes conversations from 9+ AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini, Aider, etc.) into a unified, searchable timeline. Key features:
- Sub-60ms prefix search across all agent history
- Robot mode (--robot) for JSON output
- Health checking (cass health)
- Workspace filtering

### Why integrate?
When reviewing closed issues or understanding project history, users often wonder "how did we actually solve this?" The coding sessions contain that context—the actual AI conversations where problems were discussed and solved. Correlating sessions to beads answers this question instantly.

## Critical Design Principles

### 1. Invisible When Absent
Users without cass must NEVER see error messages, "no sessions found" states, broken UI, or loading indicators for cass features. The feature must be completely invisible when cass is not available.

### 2. Non-Blocking
All cass operations happen in background goroutines. Main UI thread is never blocked. Timeouts on all external calls (5 seconds max). Graceful degradation on any error.

### 3. Additive Only
No existing functionality changes behavior. New keybindings do not conflict. Status bar additions are minimal and contextual.

## User Experience
- Status bar shows session count indicator (📎N) only when sessions exist
- Press **V** to toggle session modal with previews ("View sessions")
- History view integrates sessions in timeline alongside commits

## Key Binding Note
The 'V' key was chosen because 'C' (for Cass) is already used:
- List view: 'c' = filter to closed issues
- History view: 'C' = cycle confidence threshold

'V' = "View sessions" is semantically meaningful and available.

## Success Metrics
- Zero user-visible errors related to cass
- Sub-100ms perceived latency for cached results
- No measurable impact on startup time without cass
- All scoring thresholds are tunable for refinement

The integration surfaces AI coding sessions from cass alongside beads while remaining completely invisible when cass is unavailable. All ~100 tests pass across pkg/cass/ and integration points.

title: Implement explicit bead ID matching in commit messages
description:
# Explicit Bead ID Matching

## Context
Many developers include bead/issue IDs in commit messages:
- "fix(auth): resolve login bug [AUTH-123]"
- "Closes AUTH-123"
- "Refs: beads-456, beads-789"

This is high-confidence (90-95%) because the developer explicitly linked them.

## Pattern Matching
\`\`\`go
var beadIDPatterns = []*regexp.Regexp{
    // [ID] format
    regexp.MustCompile(\`\\[([A-Z]+-\\d+)\\]\`),
    
    // Closes/Fixes/Refs keywords
    regexp.MustCompile(\`(?i)closes?\\s+#?([A-Z]+-\\d+)\`),
    regexp.MustCompile(\`(?i)fix(?:es|ed)?\\s+#?([A-Z]+-\\d+)\`),
    regexp.MustCompile(\`(?i)refs?\\s+#?([A-Z]+-\\d+)\`),
    
    // beads-123 format
    regexp.MustCompile(\`(?i)beads?[-_](\\d+)\`),
    
    // Generic ID at word boundary
    regexp.MustCompile(\`\\b([A-Z]{2,10}-\\d+)\\b\`),
}
\`\`\`

## Finding Commits with Explicit References
\`\`\`bash
git log --grep="AUTH-123" --format="%H|%aI|%an|%ae|%s" --all
\`\`\`

## Confidence Scoring
Base: 0.90

Adjustments:
- "Closes" or "Fixes" keyword: +0.05 → 0.95
- Multiple IDs in message: -0.02 per extra ID
- ID in brackets [AUTH-123]: +0.02

## Avoiding Duplicates
If already correlated via co-committed, don't add explicit-id duplicate.
If both methods apply, keep co-committed (higher confidence).

## Configurable Patterns
Allow users to add custom patterns in .bv/config.yaml:
\`\`\`yaml
history:
  id_patterns:
    - '\\bJIRA-\\d+\\b'
    - '\\bGH-\\d+\\b'
\`\`\`

## File Location
\`pkg/correlation/explicit.go\`

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Extracts bead IDs from various message formats
2. Uses git --grep for efficient searching
3. Avoids duplicate correlations
4. Supports custom patterns from config
5. Unit tests for pattern matching

title: Implement confidence scoring model
description:
# Confidence Scoring Model

## Context
Different correlation methods have different reliability. We need a consistent model for expressing and combining confidence scores.

## Confidence Ranges by Method
| Method | Range | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| co_committed | 0.90-0.99 | Direct causation |
| explicit_id | 0.85-0.95 | Developer intent |
| temporal_author | 0.40-0.75 | Same person, right time |

## Combining Multiple Signals
If a commit matches multiple methods:
\`\`\`go
func CombineConfidence(scores []float64) float64 {
    // Use highest as base
    sort.Float64s(scores)
    base := scores[len(scores)-1]
    
    // Boost slightly for each additional signal
    for i := 0; i < len(scores)-1; i++ {
        boost := (1.0 - base) * 0.1 * scores[i]
        base += boost
    }
    
    return min(base, 0.99)
}
\`\`\`

## Filtering by Confidence
Support \`--min-confidence\` flag:
\`\`\`bash
bv --robot-history --min-confidence 0.7
\`\`\`

## Confidence Explanation
Generate human-readable explanations:
- "Changed in same commit as bead update"
- "Commit message mentions AUTH-123"
- "By bob@dev during active window"

## File Location
\`pkg/correlation/scorer.go\`

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Each method has defined confidence range
2. Multiple signals combine correctly
3. \`--min-confidence\` filter works
4. Explanations are human-readable
5. Scores are deterministic (same input = same output)

title: Define static export data structures and JSON schema
description:
# Define SQLite Export Schema and Materialized Views

## Context
Following mcp_agent_mail's proven architecture, we'll export to SQLite and query it client-side using sql.js WASM. This is more sophisticated than JSON but provides:
- Real full-text search via FTS5
- Complex queries (dependencies, blocked chains)
- Materialized views for fast common operations
- Chunked loading for large datasets
- OPFS caching for offline support

## Database Schema

### Core Tables (exported from beads)
```sql
CREATE TABLE issues (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    priority INTEGER NOT NULL,
    issue_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    assignee TEXT,
    labels TEXT, -- JSON array, indexed via FTS
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    closed_at TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE dependencies (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    issue_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    depends_on_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    type TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'blocks', 'related', 'parent-child'
    FOREIGN KEY (issue_id) REFERENCES issues(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (depends_on_id) REFERENCES issues(id)
);

-- Graph metrics (computed by bv analysis)
CREATE TABLE issue_metrics (
    issue_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    pagerank REAL,
    betweenness REAL,
    critical_path_depth INTEGER,
    triage_score REAL,
    blocks_count INTEGER,
    blocked_by_count INTEGER,
    FOREIGN KEY (issue_id) REFERENCES issues(id)
);
```

### FTS5 Full-Text Search
```sql
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE issues_fts USING fts5(
    id,
    title,
    description,
    labels,
    assignee,
    content='issues',
    content_rowid='rowid'
);

-- Triggers to keep FTS in sync (export-time only)
```

### Materialized Views
```sql
-- Denormalized issue overview (like mcp_agent_mail's message_overview_mv)
CREATE TABLE issue_overview_mv AS
SELECT 
    i.id,
    i.title,
    i.description,
    i.status,
    i.priority,
    i.issue_type,
    i.assignee,
    i.labels,
    i.created_at,
    i.updated_at,
    i.closed_at,
    m.pagerank,
    m.betweenness,
    m.critical_path_depth,
    m.triage_score,
    m.blocks_count,
    m.blocked_by_count,
    (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(depends_on_id) FROM dependencies WHERE issue_id = i.id AND type = 'blocks') as blocks_ids,
    (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(issue_id) FROM dependencies WHERE depends_on_id = i.id AND type = 'blocks') as blocked_by_ids
FROM issues i
LEFT JOIN issue_metrics m ON i.id = m.issue_id;

-- Pre-computed triage recommendations
CREATE TABLE triage_recommendations_mv AS
SELECT 
    id,
    title,
    issue_type,
    status,
    priority,
    triage_score,
    blocks_count,
    -- reasoning computed from analysis
    json_group_array(reason) as reasons
FROM (
    SELECT ... -- populated from --robot-triage output
);
```

### Performance Indexes
```sql
-- Covering indexes for common queries
CREATE INDEX idx_issues_status ON issues(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_issues_priority ON issues(priority, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_issues_updated ON issues(updated_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_issues_type_status ON issues(issue_type, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_deps_issue ON dependencies(issue_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_deps_depends ON dependencies(depends_on_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_metrics_score ON issue_metrics(triage_score DESC);
```

### Export Metadata Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE export_meta (
    key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    value TEXT
);
-- Contains: version, generated_at, git_commit, issue_count, etc.
```

## Export Optimization (from mcp_agent_mail)
```sql
-- Optimize for httpvfs streaming
PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE;  -- Single file, no WAL
PRAGMA page_size=1024;       -- Optimal for range requests
INSERT INTO issues_fts(issues_fts) VALUES('optimize');
VACUUM;
ANALYZE;
PRAGMA optimize;
```

## File Output
```
outputDir/
  beads.sqlite3              # Main database
  beads.sqlite3.config.json  # Chunk config (if chunked)
  chunks/                    # Optional chunks for large DBs
  data/
    triage.json              # Full robot-triage output
    insights.json            # Full robot-insights output
    plan.json                # Full robot-plan output
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] SQLite schema defined with all tables
- [ ] FTS5 virtual table created and populated
- [ ] Materialized views pre-computed
- [ ] Performance indexes in place
- [ ] Export metadata table populated
- [ ] Database optimized for httpvfs (page_size, VACUUM)
- [ ] Unit tests verify schema and query patterns
- [ ] Integration test with real bv data

## Why SQLite over JSON
1. **Search**: FTS5 provides real full-text search with ranking
2. **Queries**: Can express complex dependency queries in SQL
3. **Scale**: Same approach works for 50 or 50,000 issues
4. **Performance**: Client queries only what it needs, not full load
5. **Caching**: OPFS support for offline use
6. **Proven**: mcp_agent_mail demonstrates this works well
notes:
REVISION (2025-12-16): Removed SearchText field from ExportIssue.

Rationale: Pre-computing search text wastes JSON bytes. The client can build search text on load by concatenating title + description + labels. This is a one-time O(n) operation that's fast enough for <1000 issues.

Updated ExportIssue struct:
```go
type ExportIssue struct {
    model.Issue
    PageRank        float64   `json:"pagerank"`
    Betweenness     float64   `json:"betweenness,omitempty"`
    CriticalPath    int       `json:"critical_path_depth"`
    BlocksCount     int       `json:"blocks_count"`
    BlockedByCount  int       `json:"blocked_by_count"`
    BlocksIDs       []string  `json:"blocks_ids,omitempty"`
    BlockedByIDs    []string  `json:"blocked_by_ids,omitempty"`
    // SearchText removed - client computes on load
}
```

Client-side search text generation:
```javascript
function buildSearchText(issue) {
  return [
    issue.id,
    issue.title,
    issue.description || '',
    (issue.labels || []).join(' '),
    issue.assignee || ''
  ].join(' ').toLowerCase();
}
```

Implemented SQLite export schema and Go data structures:
- Created sqlite_types.go with ExportIssue, ExportDependency, ExportMetrics, ExportMeta structs

- Added comprehensive tests in sqlite_schema_test.go (all passing)
- Schema includes: issues, dependencies, issue_metrics, triage_recommendations, export_meta tables
- FTS5 full-text search support (works in sql.js browser environment)
- Materialized view issue_overview_mv for fast list queries
- Performance indexes for common query patterns
- Optimization functions for httpvfs streaming

title: CapsLock Key Detection
description:
# CapsLock Key Detection

## Background
CapsLock is a "power user" shortcut for direct tutorial access. The **primary discoverable path** is pressing `?` (help modal) then `Space` for the tutorial. CapsLock provides a quicker bypass for users who know it exists.

## Design Decision: CapsLock as Secondary Entry Point

The user flow priority is:
1. **Primary (discoverable)**: `?` → Help modal → `Space` → Tutorial
2. **Power user shortcut**: `CapsLock` → Tutorial directly
3. **Context help**: `CapsLock` double-tap → Context-specific help

This ensures users can always access the tutorial even if their terminal doesn't handle CapsLock well.

## Technical Challenge
BubbleTea represents CapsLock differently across platforms:
- Some terminals send it as a regular key event
- Some send it as a special key
- Some don't send it at all (captured by OS)
- vim users often remap CapsLock to Escape

## Implementation Strategy

### CapsLock Detection (Best Effort)
\`\`\`go
func isCapsLock(msg tea.KeyMsg) bool {
    // Terminal-dependent detection
    // May need to check msg.Type and msg.String()
    // Return false if uncertain (user can use ? → Space)
}
\`\`\`

### Double-Tap Detection
\`\`\`go
type capsLockTracker struct {
    lastPress time.Time
    threshold time.Duration // 300ms for double-tap
}

func (c *capsLockTracker) HandlePress() tutorialTrigger {
    now := time.Now()
    if now.Sub(c.lastPress) < c.threshold {
        c.lastPress = time.Time{} // Reset
        return triggerContextHelp
    }
    c.lastPress = now
    return tea.Tick(c.threshold, func(time.Time) tea.Msg {
        return capsLockTimerExpiredMsg{}
    })
}
\`\`\`

## Graceful Degradation
If CapsLock detection proves unreliable on certain terminals:
- Users always have `?` → `Space` path
- Could show hint on first run: "Tip: CapsLock opens tutorial (or use ? then Space)"
- Consider making CapsLock binding configurable

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] CapsLock detected in common terminals (iTerm2, Terminal.app, etc.)
- [ ] Double-tap within 300ms triggers context help
- [ ] Single tap triggers full tutorial after delay
- [ ] Graceful fallback when CapsLock not detected
- [ ] No interference with actual CapsLock toggle

## Testing Notes
- Document which terminals work/don't work
- Ensure ? → Space path always works as fallback

## Dependencies
None - but coordinates with Help Modal Update task.

title: Implement reverse lookup (commit → bead)
description:
# Reverse Lookup: Commit → Bead

## Context
Sometimes you're looking at a commit and want to know which bead it relates to.
"Why was this change made? What bead drove it?"

## Two Access Patterns
1. Via commit_index in HistoryReport (already built into structure)
2. Direct CLI query: \`bv --commit-bead <sha>\`

## New CLI Flag
\`\`\`bash
# Which bead(s) relate to this commit?
bv --commit-bead abc1234

# Output:
{
  "commit": "abc1234",
  "message": "fix(auth): resolve race condition",
  "related_beads": [
    {
      "bead_id": "AUTH-123",
      "bead_title": "Fix login race condition",
      "method": "co_committed",
      "confidence": 0.95
    }
  ]
}
\`\`\`

## Orphan Commit Detection
Commits that don't correlate to ANY bead:
\`\`\`go
func FindOrphanCommits(report *HistoryReport) []CommitInfo {
    correlated := make(map[string]bool)
    for sha := range report.CommitIndex {
        correlated[sha] = true
    }
    
    var orphans []CommitInfo
    for _, commit := range getAllCodeCommits() {
        if !correlated[commit.SHA] {
            orphans = append(orphans, commit)
        }
    }
    return orphans
}
\`\`\`

This is useful for code hygiene: "These commits have no associated bead!"

## Summary Stats Update
Add to HistorySummary:
- orphan_commits: Count of commits with no bead
- orphan_ratio: orphan_commits / total_commits

## File Location
- \`cmd/bv/main.go\` (new flag)
- \`pkg/correlation/reverse.go\` (lookup logic)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. \`--commit-bead <sha>\` outputs correct JSON
2. commit_index in report is accurate
3. Orphan detection works
4. Handles commits with multiple related beads
5. Handles commits with no related beads gracefully

title: Add --export-pages CLI flag and command handler
description:
# Add --export-pages CLI Flag and Command Handler

## Context
Add the core CLI interface for exporting static pages. This is the non-interactive version that can be used in CI/CD pipelines.

## Requirements

### New CLI Flags (cmd/bv/main.go)
```go
exportPages := flag.String("export-pages", "", "Export static site to directory (e.g., ./bv-pages)")
pagesTitle := flag.String("pages-title", "", "Custom title for static site")
pagesIncludeClosed := flag.Bool("pages-include-closed", false, "Include closed issues in export")
pagesMinify := flag.Bool("pages-minify", false, "Minify JSON output")
previewPages := flag.String("preview-pages", "", "Preview existing static site bundle")
```

### Command Flow
```go
if *exportPages != "" {
    config := export.ExportConfig{
        Title:         *pagesTitle,
        IncludeClosed: *pagesIncludeClosed,
        Minify:        *pagesMinify,
    }
    
    // Load issues (reuse existing loader)
    issues, err := loader.LoadFromPath(beadsPath)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    
    // Build graph (reuse existing analysis)
    graph := analysis.BuildGraph(issues)
    
    // Create exporter and run
    exporter := export.NewStaticExporter(issues, graph, config)
    if err := exporter.Export(*exportPages); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    
    fmt.Printf("✓ Static site exported to: %s\n", *exportPages)
    fmt.Printf("  Open %s/index.html in a browser to view\n", *exportPages)
    os.Exit(0)
}
```

### Preview Mode
```go
if *previewPages != "" {
    // Start local HTTP server
    server := export.NewPreviewServer(*previewPages, 9000)
    fmt.Printf("Preview server running at http://localhost:%d\n", server.Port)
    fmt.Println("Press Ctrl+C to stop")
    
    // Open browser
    browser.Open(fmt.Sprintf("http://localhost:%d", server.Port))
    
    // Block until interrupted
    server.ListenAndServe()
    os.Exit(0)
}
```

### Output Messages
```
$ bv --export-pages ./bv-pages

Exporting static site...
  → Loading issues from .beads/beads.jsonl
  → Found 178 issues (85 open, 93 closed)
  → Running graph analysis...
  → Generating triage data...
  → Writing JSON files...
  → Copying viewer assets...

✓ Static site exported to: ./bv-pages
  Files: 5 JSON data files, 4 viewer assets
  Total size: 245 KB

To preview locally:
  bv --preview-pages ./bv-pages

To deploy to GitHub Pages:
  bv --pages (interactive wizard)
```

### Error Handling
- Output directory exists: Prompt to overwrite or fail with --force
- No issues found: Warn but create empty site
- Graph analysis timeout: Use partial data with warning
- Write errors: Clean up partial output

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] --export-pages flag creates complete static site
- [ ] --preview-pages starts local server
- [ ] Output shows progress and summary
- [ ] Works in non-TTY environments (CI)
- [ ] --help shows new flags with descriptions
- [ ] Exit code 0 on success, 1 on error

## Integration Points
- Reuses existing loader, analysis, and graph code
- Hooks into robot output generation (triage, insights, plan)
- Respects BV_DATA_PATH environment variable

# History Caching Layer

title: Support incremental history updates

# Incremental History Updates

## Context
When only a few new commits exist since last cache, we shouldn't re-parse the entire history. Parse only new commits and merge.

## Algorithm
1. Find new commits since cached report (using LatestCommitSHA)
2. If few new commits (<100), parse only those
3. Merge new events with existing correlations
4. If too many new commits, full refresh is more efficient

## Track Latest Commit
Add to HistoryReport: LatestCommitSHA string

## Merge Logic
- New beads: Add to correlations
- Updated beads: Merge events, re-correlate if needed
- Existing correlations: Keep if still valid

## File Location
\`pkg/correlation/incremental.go\`

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Detects when incremental update is possible
2. Only parses new commits
3. Correctly merges with existing data
4. Falls back to full refresh when appropriate
5. Performance improvement measurable

title: Optimize for large repositories
description:
# Large Repository Optimization

## Context
For repos with 10,000+ commits, naive parsing is too slow. Need smarter strategies.

## Strategies

### 1. Default Commit Limit
\`\`\`go
const DefaultHistoryLimit = 500
\`\`\`

### 2. Streaming Parser
Don't load all git output into memory. Stream and parse line-by-line.

### 3. Parallel File Stats
Batch git show requests for multiple SHAs.

### 4. Skip Old Beads
\`--history-closed-since "90 days"\` - Only beads closed in last 90 days.

### 5. Progress Indicator
For TUI, show progress while loading:
\`\`\`
Loading history... 234/500 commits
\`\`\`

## Benchmarking Targets
- 100 commits: instant (<100ms)
- 1,000 commits: fast (<1s)
- 10,000 commits: acceptable (<5s)

## File Location
- \`pkg/correlation/stream.go\` (streaming parser)
- \`pkg/correlation/batch.go\` (batched git calls)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. 500 commit default limit
2. Streaming parser doesn't OOM
3. Batch file stats is faster than sequential
4. Progress indicator in TUI
5. Meets benchmark targets
close_reason: Implemented streaming parser with 500 default limit, batch file stats extractor, progress callback, and ClosedSince option

description:
## Overview
Detect and surface files that frequently change together across commits.

## Why Agents Need This
When an agent modifies a file, it should know what OTHER files typically change alongside it. This prevents incomplete changes and reveals hidden coupling.

## Data Available
```go
type CorrelatedCommit struct {
    Files []string  // Files changed in this commit
}
```

## Implementation

### Co-Change Analysis
- Build adjacency matrix: file A changed with file B in N commits
- Identify clusters of frequently co-changed files
- Surface as 'related files' when viewing any file's history

### Display
When viewing a file in history:
```
📁 auth/token.go
   Co-changes with (80%+ correlation):
   • auth/session.go (changed together in 12/14 commits)
   • middleware/auth.go (changed together in 9/14 commits)
   • config/auth.yaml (changed together in 7/14 commits)
```

### Robot Command Integration
`bv robot file-relations auth/token.go` → JSON of co-change patterns

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Co-change matrix computed from commit history
- [ ] Related files shown in file-centric view
- [ ] Robot command exposes data for agent consumption

title: Cass Search Interface with Safety Wrappers
description:
# Cass Search Interface with Safety Wrappers

## Purpose
Provide a safe, timeout-protected interface for searching cass. This wraps the raw CLI calls with error handling, JSON parsing, and resource management.

## Background

### Why a Wrapper?
Direct exec.Command calls are dangerous:
- No timeout protection (could hang forever)
- No error normalization (different failure modes)
- No resource limiting (could spawn too many processes)
- JSON parsing errors could crash

This wrapper provides a safe abstraction that handles all failure modes gracefully.

### cass Search Command
```bash
cass search "query" --robot --limit 10 --fields minimal --days 30
```

Flags we use:
- `--robot`: JSON output (required)
- `--limit N`: Cap results (default 10)
- `--fields minimal`: Reduce token count
- `--days N`: Time filter for relevance
- `--workspace PATH`: Filter by project (critical for relevance)

## Implementation

### Search Options
```go
type SearchOptions struct {
    Query     string        // Required: search query
    Limit     int           // Max results (default 10)
    Days      int           // Time filter (0 = no filter)
    Workspace string        // Filter by workspace path
    Fields    string        // "minimal", "summary", or field list
    Timeout   time.Duration // Override default 5s timeout
}
```

### Search Result Types
```go
type SearchResult struct {
    SourcePath  string    // Path to session file
    LineNumber  int       // Line in session
    Agent       string    // "claude", "cursor", etc.
    Title       string    // Conversation title
    Score       float64   // Relevance score (0-1)
    Snippet     string    // Content preview
    Timestamp   time.Time // When the message occurred
    MatchType   string    // "exact", "prefix", "fuzzy"
}

type SearchResponse struct {
    Results []SearchResult
    Meta    SearchMeta
}

type SearchMeta struct {
    ElapsedMs int
    Total     int
    Truncated bool
    Error     string // Non-empty if partial failure
}
```

### Safety Mechanisms

#### 1. Timeout Protection
```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "cass", args...)
```

#### 2. Concurrent Call Limiting
```go
var cassSemaphore = make(chan struct{}, 2) // Max 2 concurrent
cassSemaphore <- struct{}{}
defer func() { <-cassSemaphore }()
```

#### 3. Output Size Limiting
```go
// Limit output to 1MB to prevent memory issues
output := make([]byte, 1024*1024)
n, _ := io.ReadFull(stdout, output)
```

#### 4. Graceful JSON Parsing
```go
var resp SearchResponse
if err := json.Unmarshal(output, &resp); err != nil {
    // Try to extract partial results
    // Log error for debugging
    // Return empty response, not error
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Executes cass search with proper arguments
- [ ] Enforces timeout on all calls
- [ ] Limits concurrent cass processes
- [ ] Parses JSON response correctly
- [ ] Returns empty results (not error) on failure
- [ ] Supports workspace filtering
- [ ] Handles partial/malformed responses

## Error Handling Philosophy
NEVER bubble errors to UI. All failures result in empty results:
- Timeout → empty results, debug log
- JSON parse error → empty results, debug log
- Process crash → empty results, debug log
- No results → empty results (not "no results found")

## Testing Strategy
- Mock cass binary responses
- Test timeout behavior
- Test malformed JSON handling
- Test concurrent call limiting
- Test workspace filtering
close_reason: Implemented Cass search interface with safety wrappers: timeout protection, concurrent call limiting (semaphore), graceful JSON parsing, output size limiting. 19 new tests pass with -race.

title: Labels View & Dashboard System
description:
# Labels View & Dashboard System

## Overview
Implement a comprehensive Labels View that turns labels into a first-class organizational mechanism. This enables long-horizon task coordination by providing dashboards for feature areas (feat:auth), work types (fixes, ui), and epic progress tracking.

## Inspiration
Based on @kraitsura's Labels Viewer concept showing:
- Label selector with fuzzy search and progress bars
- Dashboard view grouping by EPICS and LABELS  
- Completion tracking (X/Y format with visual progress)
- Dependency depth toggle

## User Stories
- As a project lead, I want to see progress across feature areas at a glance
- As a developer, I want to quickly filter to issues with a specific label
- As a team, we want to track epic completion with roll-up statistics
- As anyone, I want fuzzy search to find labels quickly

## Key Features

### 1. Label Selector (Overlay)
- Fuzzy searchable picker accessible via \`l\` key from any view
- Shows all labels and epics with progress bars
- X/Y format showing completed vs total
- Checkmarks for 100% complete labels

### 2. Label Dashboard View  
- Dedicated view showing label statistics
- Two sections: EPICS (issues with type=epic) and LABELS
- Progress bars with completion percentages
- Expandable to drill into issues per label
- Section cycling: Ready/Blocked/InProgress/Closed

### 3. Dependency Depth Toggle
- \`d\` key cycles through 1/2/3/All depth levels
- Controls how deeply to show dependency chains
- Current depth shown in status bar

### 4. Visual Enhancements
- Distinction between labeled and unlabeled issues
- Epic progress roll-up from child issues
- Quick jump from dashboard to filtered list

## Keybindings
| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| l | Open label selector (global) |
| Enter | Select label / Confirm |
| Esc | Close selector / Back |
| j/k | Navigate |
| Tab | Cycle sections |
| d | Cycle dependency depth |

## Success Criteria
- [ ] \`l\` key opens label selector from any view
- [ ] Dashboard shows accurate progress for all labels
- [ ] Fuzzy search finds labels quickly
- [ ] Epic completion rolls up from children
- [ ] Dependency depth toggle works smoothly

## Implementation Phases
1. **Phase 1**: Label statistics extraction and data model
2. **Phase 2**: Label selector UI with fuzzy search
3. **Phase 3**: Label dashboard view
4. **Phase 4**: Integration, depth toggle, polish

title: Semantic Vector Search
description:
Add natural language search via vector embeddings, enabling queries like 'memory leak issues' to find relevant results even without exact keyword matches.

## Background & Motivation
Current search is regex-based, requiring exact matches. Users want to search by meaning, not just keywords. AI agents benefit from semantic retrieval for RAG patterns.

## Value Proposition
- For Humans: 'that thing about memory leaks' actually finds it
- For AI Agents: RAG over project history - 'how did we solve similar issues before?'

## Technical Approach
1. Local embeddings (start simple: sentence-transformers via subprocess or pure Go)
2. Vector storage (sqlite-vec extension or simple flat file)
3. Incremental indexing (embed on first access, update when issues change)
4. Semantic search mode in CLI and TUI

## Scope Control
Start minimal:
- Embed title + description only
- Single embedding model
- Top-10 results
- No hybrid search initially

## Dependencies & Risks
- Embedding model choice affects quality and size
- May require external tool (Python) initially
- Could start with Go-native solution later

title: Recipes match their documentation: project files, path argument, shared apply with metric sorts, view/export decision
description:
## Context
`pkg/recipe`: 11 builtins (`defaults/recipes.yaml`) verified. `Loader.Load` reads `~/.config/bv/recipes.yaml` (loader.go:69) and `<cwd>/.bv/recipes.yaml` (loader.go:99) as a `recipes:` map. title: Semantic search: ship a real embedder behind a build tag or reduce the claim to hashed vectors
description:
## Context
`pkg/search/config.go:35-47`: `NewEmbedderFromConfig` returns "not implemented (mvp placeholder)" for `python-sentence-transformers` and `openai`; only `hash` (FNV-1a feature hashing, `hash_embedder.go:39-101`) works, and `embedder.go:9-10` says it "is not a true semantic model". README "Semantic Search" describes "semantic vector search" and the env table documents `BV_SEMANTIC_EMBEDDER`/`BV_SEMANTIC_MODEL` as if providers were selectable. `docs/semantic-search-embedding.md` names sentence-transformers as the primary plan.

## Decision (record in closing comment)
Option 1 (recommended): ship a real local embedder behind a build tag: ONNX MiniLM-class model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or similar permissively licensed) through a pure-Go ONNX runtime, `BV_SEMANTIC_EMBEDDER=onnx`, model fetched on first use into the user cache dir and verified by SHA-256 (fail closed), dimension 384 matching the existing index format; `hash` stays the default so nothing changes for users who do not opt in.
Option 2: remove the two provider constants and the env rows, and reword README to "hashed keyword vectors".

## Success criteria (option 1)
- `TestONNXEmbedder_KnownVectors` against a checked-in small fixture; `TestNewEmbedderFromConfig_AllListedProvidersConstruct`.
- e2e: with the onnx embedder, a query "authentication" ranks an issue titled "login flow" above one titled "graph layout".
- `.bvvi` index records provider and dimension; mixing providers rebuilds the index.
- README and docs/semantic-search-embedding.md updated by the docs epic.
close_reason: I3 decision: option 2. README 'Semantic Search' and the env table now say the vectors are FNV-1a hashed keyword features (pkg/search/hash_embedder.go), that only BV_SEMANTIC_EMBEDDER=hash is implemented, and that python-sentence-transformers/openai are reserved names that fail with 'not implemented'. The provider constants stay because config tests assert that exact failure. No ONNX embedder shipped: it would add a model download + runtime for a feature nobody has asked for; revisit on demand.

title: Export claims made true: hybrid WASM switch, self-contained graph HTML, measured pages numbers, pages branch behaviour
description:
## Context
Export claims versus code (verified 2026-09-01):
- `BV_BUILD_HYBRID_WASM=1 bv --export-pages` cannot work in a built binary: `maybeBuildHybridWasmAssets` is called only in the filesystem-fallback branch (cmd/bv/main.go:6565-6571) after `export.HasEmbeddedAssets()` returned at 6560-6562; assets are always embedded (`viewer_embed.go:21-22`).
- The hybrid scorer WASM is only attempted at `issueCount >= 5000` (`viewer_assets/wasm_loader.js:5, 58-61`), undocumented.
- `--export-graph` HTML links Google Fonts (`graph_render_beautiful.go:21`) although README says "completely self-contained"; the file is 1.6 MB here versus "400KB-1MB"; README says "WebGL-accelerated" but the vendored force-graph uses Canvas 2D.
- Pages "16x faster / 4 s to ~250 ms / 82 KB vs 914 KB" appear only in README; the originating commit and `sqlite_export.go:867` say ~30 KB vs ~200 KB; the real `graph_layout.json` is 101,823 B for 541 nodes. Force simulation still runs warmup/cooldown ticks (graph.js:802-803) even with pinned positions.
- `--pages` pushes `main` plus a SHA-pinned Actions workflow (github.go:295-397); `gh-pages` only in the rate-limit fallback (954-975); README says it auto-creates gh-pages.

## Target state
- The build hook runs before the embedded copy when the env var is set and writes into the bundle's `wasm/`; the threshold becomes `BV_HYBRID_WASM_MIN_ISSUES` (default 5000) and is documented; or the feature is removed with the env var and script (decide, record).
- Graph export inlines the two font faces as base64 `@font-face` data URIs (Inter and JetBrains Mono subsets) or drops the link; `TestGraphHTML_HasNoExternalRequests` greps `src=`/`href=` for `http`.
- `tests/e2e/pages_perf_test.go` writes `tests/artifacts/perf/pages_load.json` (layout bytes, sqlite bytes, and, when a headless browser is available via `BV_HEADLESS_BROWSER`, time-to-first-render); README numbers come from that file (docs epic).
- README "Deployment Options" and "Interactive Wizard" describe the main-plus-workflow flow and the fallback.

## Success criteria
- `TestExportPages_BuildsHybridWasmWhenRequested` (skips with a logged reason when wasm-pack is absent).
- `TestGraphHTML_HasNoExternalRequests`.
- `pages_load.json` produced in the e2e run.
close_reason: I4: graph HTML export makes no external requests (Google Fonts link removed; TestGraphHTML_HasNoExternalRequests); BV_BUILD_HYBRID_WASM now runs in the released binary (build hook moved after the embedded-asset copy, writes into <bundle>/wasm, fails loudly without wasm-pack or the source checkout; e2e TestExportPages_HybridWasmHookRunsInBuiltBinary covers the error path, skipping when wasm-pack is installed); tests/e2e TestExportPages_RecordsLoadSizes writes tests/artifacts/perf/pages_load.json (611 issues: sqlite 3.3 MB, layout 116 KB, bundle 9.7 MB) and README cites it. Decisions: the 5,000-issue WASM threshold stays a documented constant (no env var); force-simulation warmup ticks left as is; first-render timing not implemented (the JSON says so rather than inventing a number); pages branch behaviour was already documented correctly.

title: Forecast and capacity: implement list scheduling over the dependency DAG (or document the heuristic honestly)
description:
## Context
`--robot-forecast` and `--robot-capacity` (pkg/analysis/eta.go:94-258; cmd/bv/robot_registry.go:3119-3300) estimate duration as 60 min default x type multiplier x depth x description-length factor, velocity as closed-in-30-days minutes / 30, confidence by rules, and capacity as `serial + parallel/agents`; `summary.total_days` ignores the agent count. README "ETA Forecasting & Capacity Planning" and the robot table call this "dependency-aware scheduling" and "team capacity simulation". `--forecast-agents=N` exists.

## Decision (record in closing comment)
Option 1 (recommended): implement list scheduling: topological order over the non-closed dependency DAG, critical-path-first priority, N agents, each issue assigned to the earliest-free agent after its prerequisites finish; output per-agent timelines, makespan, and per-issue start/finish; `--forecast-agents` and `--agents` drive it; the plan view's tracks become the natural partition.
Option 2: keep the heuristic and rewrite the README to describe it as such.

## Success criteria (option 1)
- `TestCapacity_ListSchedulingRespectsDependencies`: no issue starts before its blockers finish.
- `TestForecast_AgentsReduceMakespan`: makespan(2 agents) <= makespan(1 agent) and equals the critical path when agents >= width.
- e2e `robot_capacity_test.go` and `robot_forecast` cases updated; payloads include `schedule` and `assumptions` (default minutes, multipliers).
close_reason: I5 decision: option 2. README robot tables and the 'ETA Forecasting & Capacity Planning' section now describe the real heuristic (estimated_minutes or median x type weight x depth factor up to 2x x description factor; velocity = closed minutes/day over 30 days with median/5 and 60 min/day fallbacks; ETA = minutes/(velocity x agents); capacity = serial + parallel/agents, no per-agent assignment) and state it is not a scheduler; AGENTS.md row matches; payload 'factors' make the numbers auditable. List scheduling is left as a future feature.

title: TOON output: measure against JSON per command, document where it helps, make --stats honest
description:
## Context
`--format toon` is real (toon-go shells out to the `tru`/`toon` CLI; falls back to JSON with a stderr warning when absent). README and AGENTS.md present TOON as "token-optimized output for lower LLM context usage". Measured on this repository: `--robot-triage --stats` reported TOON approximately 2,668 tokens versus JSON approximately 2,354 (TOON larger). `--stats` prints only with the flag.

## Target state
Measure TOON versus JSON token estimates across every robot command on the synthetic fixture and this repository; record the table in `tests/artifacts/perf/toon_vs_json.md`; document in README where TOON helps (wide tabular payloads such as `--robot-graph`, `--robot-label-health`) and where it does not (nested triage); make `--stats` print both sizes and the ratio; consider auto-selecting JSON when TOON is larger (`--format auto`), decide and record.

## Success criteria
- `tests/e2e/toon_size_test.go` produces the table and fails if TOON is more than 10 percent larger for a command README lists as a TOON win.
close_reason: I6: measured on this repo (tests/artifacts/perf/toon_vs_json.md): TOON is 7% smaller for --robot-graph, about equal for --robot-next/--robot-alerts, and 9-15% larger for --robot-label-health, --robot-insights, --robot-triage, --robot-plan. README/AGENTS.md/blurb now recommend TOON only for wide tabular payloads and point at --stats; --stats printed '0% savings' when TOON was larger (guard suppressed negatives) and now prints 'TOON N% larger/smaller'. tests/e2e/toon_size_test.go re-measures and fails if a documented TOON win grows past 110% of JSON. No auto-switch to JSON: --format is an explicit request.

title: Port TopK Set (greedy submodular selection) to Rust WASM
notes:
PERFORMANCE NOTE: Current implementation calls what_if_close() for every open node in each iteration. For n nodes and k iterations: O(n*k) calls. Each what_if is O(n), so total is O(n²*k).

For 1000 nodes, k=10: ~10M operations.

OPTIMIZATION OPPORTUNITY: Memoize/cache what-if results, or use incremental updates as nodes are 'closed' during selection.
close_reason: Implemented TopK Set greedy submodular selection in Rust WASM. Uses what_if_close for cascade impact, properly marks cascade nodes as covered. 13 tests, all 202 WASM tests pass. WASM bindings: topkSet, topkSetDefault.

close_reason: Implemented eigenvector centrality with power iteration. Correctly handles DAGs (converges to uniform) and cyclic graphs. Added WASM bindings. 10 tests pass.

title: [RC-P1] Turn 10k responsiveness and ranking claims into measured acceptance
description:
## Observed gap and background
README calls TUI glitch-free 60fps and describes 10,000-issue virtualization. Existing TestPerf_LargeDatasetLatency uses only 500 issues. Audit RCH microbenchmarks: 10k graph rebuild 8.23–14.37ms/op, View 5.05–9.47ms/op; 614-record full analysis 27.23–30.66ms/op. Three rounds of three iterations are encouraging, not p99 input-to-paint or regression proof. Older v0.22 notes record update+render p99 about 33–36ms, above a 16.67ms frame budget.

## Required implementation
Extend existing performance harness and artifacts with frozen/hash-identified 1k/5k/10k realistic and adversarial graph workloads. Measure cold process/cache separately from warm CLI, plus key update+render during concurrent snapshot refresh, memory/GC and metric degradation. Set explicit reference-host acceptance for ordinary navigation and background interaction; distinguish 60fps rendering target from a broader 50ms interaction SLO. Qualify universal README language to measured guarantees. Optimize only profiled misses and preserve result parity. For search, report that ranked keyword behavior is evaluated separately from speed; do not infer semantic quality from a timing pass.

## Verification and acceptance
Independent warmed/cold cohorts, reproducible graph seeds, fixed clock where semantics require it, minimum meaningful samples for p50/p95/p99, repeated baseline/current pairs on same host, and output equivalence including status. Cases: deep chain, wide DAG, cyclic/dense, many closed issues, long Unicode text and rapid refresh. Inject a slow handler to prove the gate can fail; a skipped metric must not count as a fast successful calculation.

## Delivery constraints
Work in existing implementation/test files where sensible. Do not delete files, rewrite unrelated work, create compatibility shims, or run browser-opening product actions. Build, vet, first-party formatting and relevant tests must pass after implementation. Retain concise failing-before/passing-after evidence with source revision, fixture identity, command, exit code and observed-versus-expected results. The companion test bead is required for completion of this gap.
design: Ambition rounds: compare quality and latency together. Frozen dataset and configuration/clock, permutations, same-host alternating baseline/current cohorts, cold/warm separation, adequate samples for tail percentiles. Full result parity includes statuses; a timeout is not faster successful work. Profile only reproducible misses. A 16.67ms 60fps budget differs from the established 50ms interaction budget. Qualify docs by workload and percentiles. Treat noisy regression results as inconclusive, not permission to raise limits.

title: [RC-P5 proof] Verify ranking quality metrics and independent query expectations
description:
## Background
Vision checklist row 22 remains UNPROVEN: current hash-vector and hybrid tests establish scoring mechanics and deterministic output, but no judged corpus establishes useful ranking at scale. Search intentionally uses FNV-1a keyword features; learned semantic embeddings remain a recorded scope reduction in bv-9hti.3. Passing latency/parity tests cannot show whether users find the right issue.

## Required implementation
Extend existing search testdata/evaluation harness with at least 30 public or synthetic, reviewable query intents and judged relevant issue IDs, covering exact ID, multiword keyword, short/prefix, Unicode, similarly titled issues, status/priority-driven hybrid presets and no-match cases. Keep evaluation expectations independent from scorer output. Separate an evaluation subset from tuning examples. Record recall@10 and nDCG@10 plus exact-ID success by query class, corpus/source hash, preset/weights and scale (including 5k/10k distractors). Establish baseline before tuning; investigate concrete relevance regressions while keeping narrowed keyword semantics. Do not promise synonym/learned semantic understanding, fabricate human judgments, or tune thresholds merely to obtain a pass.

## Acceptance and tests
Holdout-like immutable query fixtures with independently reasoned relevance labels, exact-ID rank-one assertion, empty/no-match behavior, score ties and deterministic ordering. Negative control shuffles/zeros ranking and must lower quality metrics or fail the exact-ID contract. Test metric calculation against hand-computed small examples. Compare text and hybrid presets separately; benchmark latency stays in P1. If subjective usefulness requires human judgment, mark that portion explicitly unproven and preserve the concrete questions rather than label automated assertions human validation.

## Constraints
Use existing search/testdata files where practical. No customer data, external model service, package-manager addition, production index replacement or deletion. Save corpus/query/expectation hashes and per-query results so aggregate scores cannot conceal a failed important query. Record current performance independently; this task is quality proof, not a new search architecture.

## Independent proof ownership
This companion independently reviews expectation labels and hand-computed metric examples, drives the real CLI for representative corpus queries, and exercises the deliberately broken ranking. Do not derive relevance labels from the implementation under test. Missing human review is not a passing subjective-usability claim.

- [ ] At least 30 independently reasoned query expectations cover the specified query classes.
- [ ] Recall@10/nDCG@10 calculations match hand-computed examples and broken ranking is detected.
- [ ] Text/hybrid results and 5k/10k distractor runs include per-query IDs and corpus/config identity.
- [ ] Any unperformed human relevance review is explicitly unproven; no learned-semantic claim is introduced.

title: [RC-P1 proof] Prove reproducible latency, memory and result-quality gates
description:
## Independent proof target
README calls TUI glitch-free 60fps and describes 10,000-issue virtualization. Existing TestPerf_LargeDatasetLatency uses only 500 issues. Audit RCH microbenchmarks: 10k graph rebuild 8.23–14.37ms/op, View 5.05–9.47ms/op; 614-record full analysis 27.23–30.66ms/op. Three rounds of three iterations are encouraging, not p99 input-to-paint or regression proof. Older v0.22 notes record update+render p99 about 33–36ms, above a 16.67ms frame budget.

## Behavior that must be established
Extend existing performance harness and artifacts with frozen/hash-identified 1k/5k/10k realistic and adversarial graph workloads. Measure cold process/cache separately from warm CLI, plus key update+render during concurrent snapshot refresh, memory/GC and metric degradation. Set explicit reference-host acceptance for ordinary navigation and background interaction; distinguish 60fps rendering target from a broader 50ms interaction SLO. Qualify universal README language to measured guarantees. Optimize only profiled misses and preserve result parity. For search, report that ranked keyword behavior is evaluated separately from speed; do not infer semantic quality from a timing pass.

## Required unit/integration/E2E coverage
Independent warmed/cold cohorts, reproducible graph seeds, fixed clock where semantics require it, minimum meaningful samples for p50/p95/p99, repeated baseline/current pairs on same host, and output equivalence including status. Cases: deep chain, wide DAG, cyclic/dense, many closed issues, long Unicode text and rapid refresh. Inject a slow handler to prove the gate can fail; a skipped metric must not count as a fast successful calculation.

## Test workmanship and closure
Extend existing test files and harnesses. Test public behavior with a deliberately broken case/old-code negative control; do not merely mirror the implementation or assert keys exist. Log fixture/seed, source revision, argv, relevant nonsecret environment, expected and observed IDs/state, stdout/stderr and exit code on failures. Preserve artifacts for diagnosis. Run focused tests plus existing affected-package suite; use race tests for shared state and real platform/browser execution only where this task requires it. Never count a skipped prerequisite or missing runner as passed. This proof task depends on bv-apal.1; it can be designed beforehand but closes only after the real implementation and evidence succeed.
design: Ambition rounds: compare quality and latency together. Frozen dataset and configuration/clock, permutations, same-host alternating baseline/current cohorts, cold/warm separation, adequate samples for tail percentiles. Full result parity includes statuses; a timeout is not faster successful work. Profile only reproducible misses. A 16.67ms 60fps budget differs from the established 50ms interaction budget. Qualify docs by workload and percentiles. Treat noisy regression results as inconclusive, not permission to raise limits.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] Independently verify: Frozen 1k/5k/10k workloads have separate cold/warm and update+render distributions with source/host/seed identity.
- [x] Independently verify: Parity checks include selected IDs/order and metric status so timeout cannot masquerade as a speedup.
- [x] Independently verify: A deliberate slowdown trips the gate; docs distinguish frame-rate target from measured interaction latency.
- [x] Capture positive and negative control evidence with source revision, fixture, argv, expected/observed values and failure artifacts.
- [ ] Required real-service/platform/browser runs are completed where specified; no skipped prerequisite is marked passed.
notes: Refinement 4: P5 (bv-apal.9/bv-apal.10) now owns judged retrieval relevance. This task owns performance and behavior preservation only; avoid duplicate quality-oracle work. Record distributions as descriptive evidence unless sample size/design justifies stronger statistical claims.

title: [RC-P5] Evaluate keyword and hybrid relevance on an independently judged query corpus
description:
## Background
Vision checklist row 22 remains UNPROVEN: current hash-vector and hybrid tests establish scoring mechanics and deterministic output, but no judged corpus establishes useful ranking at scale. Search intentionally uses FNV-1a keyword features; learned semantic embeddings remain a recorded scope reduction in bv-9hti.3. Passing latency/parity tests cannot show whether users find the right issue.

## Required implementation
Extend existing search testdata/evaluation harness with at least 30 public or synthetic, reviewable query intents and judged relevant issue IDs, covering exact ID, multiword keyword, short/prefix, Unicode, similarly titled issues, status/priority-driven hybrid presets and no-match cases. Keep evaluation expectations independent from scorer output. Separate an evaluation subset from tuning examples. Record recall@10 and nDCG@10 plus exact-ID success by query class, corpus/source hash, preset/weights and scale (including 5k/10k distractors). Establish baseline before tuning; investigate concrete relevance regressions while keeping narrowed keyword semantics. Do not promise synonym/learned semantic understanding, fabricate human judgments, or tune thresholds merely to obtain a pass.

## Acceptance and tests
Holdout-like immutable query fixtures with independently reasoned relevance labels, exact-ID rank-one assertion, empty/no-match behavior, score ties and deterministic ordering. Negative control shuffles/zeros ranking and must lower quality metrics or fail the exact-ID contract. Test metric calculation against hand-computed small examples. Compare text and hybrid presets separately; benchmark latency stays in P1. If subjective usefulness requires human judgment, mark that portion explicitly unproven and preserve the concrete questions rather than label automated assertions human validation.

## Constraints
Use existing search/testdata files where practical. No customer data, external model service, package-manager addition, production index replacement or deletion. Save corpus/query/expectation hashes and per-query results so aggregate scores cannot conceal a failed important query. Record current performance independently; this task is quality proof, not a new search architecture.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] At least 30 independently reasoned query expectations cover the specified query classes.
- [ ] Recall@10/nDCG@10 calculations match hand-computed examples and broken ranking is detected.
- [ ] Text/hybrid results and 5k/10k distractor runs include per-query IDs and corpus/config identity.
- [ ] Any unperformed human relevance review is explicitly unproven; no learned-semantic claim is introduced.

title: Interactive Graph Visualization with Force-Graph
description:
# Interactive Graph Visualization with Force-Graph

## Vision
Transform the static viewer from a simple table into an **immersive, interactive graph exploration experience**. Using [force-graph](https://github.com/vasturiano/force-graph) (WebGL-accelerated), users can explore their dependency graph visually, see patterns at a glance, and perform what-if analysis with beautiful animations.

## Why This Matters

### Current State: Tables Are Limiting
- Users scroll through lists, mentally reconstructing relationships
- Hard to see the "big picture" of work
- Bottlenecks and cycles are numbers, not visible patterns
- No way to explore "what if I close this?"

### Future State: Visual Graph Intelligence
- **See the shape** of your work at a glance
- **Spot bottlenecks** as large, central nodes
- **Find cycles** as visual loops
- **Explore what-if** by clicking nodes and watching cascades
- **Understand priority** through size, color, position

## Core Features

### 1. Force-Directed Dependency Graph
- Nodes = issues, sized by impact (PageRank/blocker count)
- Edges = dependencies with directional arrows
- Colors: green (closed), blue (open), orange (blocked), red (critical)
- Smooth WebGL rendering for 1000+ nodes at 60fps
- Click node to focus, hover for tooltip, drag to reorganize

### 2. Visual What-If Analysis
- Click any open issue to "simulate close"
- Watch downstream unblocks animate (ripple effect)
- See parallelization gain visually
- Color transitions: blocked→unblocked nodes glow green
- Reset button to restore original state

### 3. Smart Clustering
- Automatic grouping by label using force clustering
- Label "galaxies" with distinct colors
- Cross-label edges show integration points
- Expand/collapse clusters
- Mini-map for navigation

### 4. Critical Path Highlighting
- Toggle to highlight longest dependency chain
- Animate path traversal
- Show "time to completion" along path
- Compare multiple paths

### 5. Time Travel Animation
- Scrubber to move through git history
- Watch graph grow/shrink over time
- See issues appear, get worked on, close
- Playback controls (play, pause, speed)

## Technical Architecture

### Library Choice: force-graph
- **Why**: WebGL-accelerated, handles 10k+ nodes, excellent API
- **CDN**: `https://unpkg.com/force-graph`
- **Alternative**: 3d-force-graph for even cooler 3D view
- **Fallback**: vis-network if WebGL unavailable

### Data Flow
```
SQLite → JS → WASM (metrics) → force-graph (render)
                ↓
         User interaction
                ↓
         WASM (what-if) → Animated update
```

### Performance Targets
- Initial render: <500ms for 500 nodes
- What-if calculation + animation: <100ms
- Smooth 60fps during interaction
- Memory: <100MB for 1000-node graph

## Visual Design Principles

1. **Clarity**: Important things are bigger, brighter
2. **Consistency**: Same colors mean same things everywhere
3. **Delight**: Smooth animations, satisfying interactions
4. **Accessibility**: Colorblind-safe palette, keyboard nav

## Success Metrics
- Users can identify top bottleneck in <5 seconds
- What-if takes <2 clicks to understand impact
- 90%+ of users prefer graph view over table for exploration
- Zero WebGL crashes/freezes

## Dependencies
- WASM Graph Engine (bv-5mgw) for metrics
- SQLite viewer infrastructure
- Static export with dependency data

## References
- force-graph: https://github.com/vasturiano/force-graph
- 3d-force-graph: https://github.com/vasturiano/3d-force-graph
- D3 force simulation: https://d3js.org/d3-force
- Graph viz inspiration: https://observablehq.com/@d3/force-directed-graph

title: Cass Result Caching System
description:
# Cass Result Caching System

## Purpose
Avoid redundant cass searches by caching correlation results. Critical for performance—without caching, navigating the issue list would trigger many slow external calls.

## Background

### Why Cache?
- cass searches take 50-500ms each
- Users navigate between beads frequently
- Same bead is often selected multiple times
- Correlation results change slowly (sessions rarely deleted)

### Cache Requirements
- Fast lookup (sub-ms)
- Bounded memory (max 100 entries)
- Automatic expiration (10-minute TTL)
- Thread-safe (concurrent UI access)
- LRU eviction (keep most recently used)

## Implementation

### Cache Structure
```go
type CacheEntry struct {
    Hint      *CorrelationHint
    CachedAt  time.Time
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

type Cache struct {
    entries map[string]*CacheEntry  // key = bead ID
    order   []string                 // LRU order (newest at end)
    maxSize int
    ttl     time.Duration
    mu      sync.RWMutex
}
```

### Cache Operations
```go
// Get returns cached hint or nil if miss/expired
func (c *Cache) Get(beadID string) *CorrelationHint

// Set stores a correlation hint
func (c *Cache) Set(beadID string, hint *CorrelationHint)

// Invalidate removes a specific entry
func (c *Cache) Invalidate(beadID string)

// Clear removes all entries
func (c *Cache) Clear()

// Stats returns cache statistics (for debugging)
func (c *Cache) Stats() CacheStats
```

### Eviction Policy
When cache is full:
1. Remove expired entries first
2. If still full, remove least recently used
3. Never exceed maxSize

### Cache Key Design
Simple: use bead ID directly (`"bv-abc123"`)

Could extend later with workspace prefix if supporting multiple projects.

## Configuration
```go
const (
    DefaultCacheSize = 100       // Max entries
    DefaultCacheTTL  = 10 * time.Minute
)
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] LRU eviction works correctly
- [ ] TTL expiration works
- [ ] Thread-safe for concurrent access
- [ ] Get/Set operations are O(1) for hit
- [ ] Memory bounded by maxSize
- [ ] Clear operation works

## Testing Strategy
- Test cache hit/miss
- Test TTL expiration
- Test LRU eviction order
- Test concurrent access (race detector)
- Benchmark operations
close_reason: Implemented LRU cache with TTL expiration, bounded memory (100 entries max), O(1) Get/Set, thread-safe concurrent access. 19 cache tests pass with -race.

title: Background Snapshot Worker Architecture for Sub-50ms UI Responsiveness
description:
# Background Snapshot Worker Architecture

## Problem Statement

When multiple AI agents are actively modifying beads.jsonl concurrently, the bv TUI becomes extremely sluggish. Analysis shows the UI thread is blocked 170-350ms per reload cycle, and with agents writing every ~50ms, the UI can be unresponsive 50-66% of the time.

## Root Cause Analysis

The current architecture performs ALL work synchronously on the UI thread when a file change is detected:

1. **File I/O** (10-100ms): Reading beads.jsonl from disk
2. **JSON Parsing** (50-500ms): Line-by-line JSONL parsing
3. **Phase 1 Analysis** (10-100ms): Degree centrality, topo sort, density
4. **Sub-view Rebuild** (50-300ms): List items, board, tree, graph, insights

**Total blocking time per reload: 170ms - 1+ second**

The existing 200-250ms debounce coalesces rapid writes but doesn't solve the fundamental problem: the reload itself blocks the event loop, preventing keyboard/mouse input processing and rendering.

## Solution: Double-Buffered Background Processing

The core insight is **separation of concerns**:
- UI thread: ONLY handles events and renders pre-computed data
- Background worker: ALL I/O, parsing, analysis, and view pre-computation

**Key Architectural Pattern: Atomic Pointer Swap**
- Background worker builds a complete, immutable DataSnapshot
- When ready, UI receives a message and swaps a single pointer (~1 nanosecond)
- UI continues using old snapshot until new one is fully ready
- Result: UI is NEVER blocked for more than a few microseconds

## Coalescing Strategy

When agents write faster than we can process:
1. First write triggers background processing
2. Subsequent writes set a "dirty" flag (doesn't interrupt processing)
3. When processing completes, check dirty flag
4. If dirty: loop and re-process with latest data
5. If clean: send snapshot to UI

This prevents queue buildup and ensures UI always gets reasonably fresh data without being overwhelmed.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] UI responsiveness < 50ms under any write load (aspirational target)
- [ ] No perceptible lag when navigating during heavy concurrent writes
- [ ] Keyboard input processed within 16ms (60fps target)
- [ ] Memory usage remains stable (no unbounded growth)
- [ ] GC pauses < 10ms during interaction

## Implementation Phases

1. **Core Infrastructure**: DataSnapshot struct, BackgroundWorker type, coalescing state machine
2. **Background Loading**: Move I/O, parsing, Phase 1 to background
3. **Pre-computed Views**: Build all view data in background
4. **GC Optimizations**: Object pooling, slice reuse, GOGC tuning
5. **Incremental Updates** (future): Change detection, partial rebuilds

## Technical Context

- Current file: pkg/watcher/watcher.go (fsnotify + debounce)
- Current handler: pkg/ui/model.go Update() case FileChangedMsg (lines 1184-1380)
- Current loader: pkg/loader/loader.go LoadIssuesFromFileWithOptions()
- Current analysis: pkg/analysis/graph.go AnalyzeAsync() (Phase 1 sync, Phase 2 async)

## Dependencies

This epic blocks any work that requires responsive UI during multi-agent scenarios.
notes: Final aggregate evidence (2026-08-25): double-buffered worker, immutable snapshots, coalescing, precomputed views, pooled loading, idle GC, and incremental list updates are implemented. Final RCH gates: changed 1000-issue SnapshotReadyMsg 4.076-4.284us/op (5x), input-only keypress Update p99 148-160us (5x, far below 16ms), keypress+full-render p99 33.05-35.54ms (3x, below 50ms), and isolated rapid-load GC pauses 0.879-1.374ms (3x, below 10ms). Snapshot/incremental race suite passed 3x; broad UI suite passed with four pre-identified RCH environment/timing-contaminated tests explicitly skipped; full remote build and vet passed. A saturated-worker broad run had one 172ms GC outlier, but fresh isolated healthy-worker runs resolved it at <1.4ms. Memory evidence: pooled parser ~3.1% fewer allocations/~2.2% fewer bytes than unpooled; final swap bytes fell from ~198KB/op to 448B/op. No unbounded-growth signal in worker stress tests.
close_reason: Completed: sub-50ms architecture proven with 4.076-4.284us snapshot swaps, 148-160us input p99, 33.05-35.54ms input+render p99, and 0.879-1.374ms GC pauses.

title: Gate stage 8: compare against a contemporaneous reference build, not a stored baseline alone
description: Stage 8 failed three times on 2026-09-02/03 while the code had not regressed: an A/B of BenchmarkParseIssuesPoolComparison on the commit before and after the loader landing measured 11.65 vs 11.66 ms, while the stored baseline (taken when the shared VM was ~35% faster) read 8.45 ms. A stored baseline cannot separate host drift from code regressions on a shared machine. Target: scripts/benchmark.sh compare also builds and runs the tracked benchmarks for the baseline's recorded commit (header line 'commit:') in a detached worktree, interleaved with HEAD on the same machine, and judges the regression from that reference run; the stored file stays as documentation and as the fallback when the worktree cannot be created (BENCH_REFERENCE=stored). Success: the comparator self-test still passes; 'compare' on a clean tree reports the reference commit and a delta near 0% during the same host conditions that produced +38% against the stored file.
design: 2026-09-03: a638efeb built the baseline commit (from the '# commit:' header) in a detached worktree and ran it before HEAD; the first live run still showed -31%..+32% deltas because load on the shared VM changes minute to minute. 356d152a interleaves the two trees per package per round (3 rounds) and switches the comparator to the best observed time per side (contention only inflates; a regression raises every sample). Self-test covers: identical, +10% noise, doubled-in-every-run (red), one contended sample (green), missing benchmark (red), BENCH_PCT honoured. Stored baseline remains the fallback (BENCH_REFERENCE=stored or commit not in clone). Second live run in progress; closure needs its worst delta near 0% under the same host conditions.
close_reason: Done (a638efeb, 356d152a, 995f566f). compare builds the baseline commit in a detached worktree, alternates ref/HEAD per package with the pair order swapped each of 4 rounds, and compares best-of-N. Live runs on the shared VM, same code in pkg/analysis on both sides: sequential ref-then-HEAD gave -31%..+32%; interleaved ref-first gave +10..+20% on identical code (ordering bias); alternating order gave +1.4/+0.8/-2.8/+1.2/-0.0% on five analysis benchmarks and -5.6%/-1.5% on the loader parse that had failed three gates; the two sub-millisecond benchmarks still swing about 15% (Sparse100 +16.5%, SnapshotSwap/100 -15.2%), worst +16.5% under the 20% threshold. Stage 8 now takes about 8 minutes. Self-test covers identical, +10% noise, doubled-in-every-run (red), one contended sample (green), missing benchmark (red), BENCH_PCT honoured. Stored baseline remains the fallback. Self-reviewed.

title: Set up Rust WASM crate with wasm-bindgen
description:
# Set up Rust WASM Crate with wasm-bindgen

## Context
This is the foundational task for the Rust WASM graph engine. We need a properly configured Rust workspace that compiles to WASM and integrates with the bv build system.

## Requirements

### Cargo.toml
```toml
[package]
name = "bv-graph-wasm"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
authors = ["bv contributors"]
description = "High-performance graph algorithms for bv static viewer"
repository = "https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer"
license = "MIT"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[features]
default = ["console_error_panic_hook"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"
js-sys = "0.3"
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
console_error_panic_hook = { version = "0.1", optional = true }

[dev-dependencies]
wasm-bindgen-test = "0.3"

[profile.release]
# Optimize for size - critical for WASM bundles
opt-level = "s"
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"
```

### Directory Structure
```
bv-graph-wasm/
  Cargo.toml
  Makefile                    # Build commands
  src/
    lib.rs                    # WASM entry point, panic hook
    graph.rs                  # DiGraph struct
    algorithms/
      mod.rs                  # Algorithm module exports
      pagerank.rs
      betweenness.rs
      eigenvector.rs
      hits.rs
      topo.rs
      cycles.rs
      critical_path.rs
      kcore.rs
      articulation.rs
      slack.rs
      density.rs
      degree.rs
    advanced/
      mod.rs
      topk_set.rs             # Greedy submodular selection
      coverage.rs             # Vertex cover
      k_paths.rs              # K-shortest paths
      parallel_cut.rs         # Parallelization analysis
      cycle_break.rs          # Cycle break suggestions
    whatif.rs                 # Impact simulation
    subgraph.rs               # Subgraph operations
    reachability.rs           # Reachability queries
  tests/
    web.rs                    # WASM integration tests
    algorithms/               # Algorithm unit tests
```

### lib.rs Skeleton
```rust
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

mod graph;
mod algorithms;
mod advanced;
mod whatif;
mod subgraph;
mod reachability;

pub use graph::DiGraph;

// Initialize panic hook for better error messages in browser console
#[wasm_bindgen(start)]
pub fn init() {
    #[cfg(feature = "console_error_panic_hook")]
    console_error_panic_hook::set_once();
}

// Re-export main types for JavaScript
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn version() -> String {
    env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").to_string()
}
```

### Makefile
```makefile
.PHONY: build build-release test clean

# Development build (faster, larger)
build:
	wasm-pack build --target web --dev

# Release build (optimized)
build-release:
	wasm-pack build --target web --release
	wasm-opt -Os -o pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg_opt.wasm pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg.wasm
	mv pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg_opt.wasm pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg.wasm

# Run tests (in browser via wasm-pack)
test:
	wasm-pack test --headless --firefox

# Clean build artifacts
clean:
	cargo clean
	rm -rf pkg/

# Check size
size:
	@echo "WASM size:"
	@wc -c pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg.wasm
	@echo "Gzipped:"
	@gzip -c pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg.wasm | wc -c
```

### Integration with bv Build System
Add to main Makefile:
```makefile
wasm:
	cd bv-graph-wasm && make build-release
	cp bv-graph-wasm/pkg/bv_graph_wasm.js pkg/export/viewer_assets/vendor/bv_graph.js
	cp bv-graph-wasm/pkg/bv_graph_wasm_bg.wasm pkg/export/viewer_assets/vendor/bv_graph_bg.wasm
```

### Prerequisites Check
```bash
# Required tools
rustup --version          # Rust toolchain
cargo --version           # Rust package manager
wasm-pack --version       # WASM build tool
wasm-opt --version        # Binaryen optimizer (optional but recommended)
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cargo.toml configured with wasm-bindgen
- [ ] Directory structure created
- [ ] lib.rs compiles with `wasm-pack build`
- [ ] Output files generated in pkg/
- [ ] Makefile works for build/test/clean
- [ ] Release build produces <150KB WASM
- [ ] Integration with bv main Makefile
- [ ] README.md documents build process

## Why This Structure?
1. **Separate crate**: Clean boundary, independent testing
2. **wasm-pack**: Standard Rust→WASM tooling
3. **wasm-opt**: Critical for size reduction (often 30-50% smaller)
4. **cdylib**: Required for WASM target
5. **console_error_panic_hook**: Better debugging in browser
6. **Module organization**: Matches Go pkg/analysis/ structure
notes: IMPORTANT: Use serde-wasm-bindgen instead of deprecated JsValue::from_serde. Add to Cargo.toml: serde-wasm-bindgen = "0.6". Use serde_wasm_bindgen::to_value() for JSON serialization to JS.
close_reason: Implemented Rust WASM crate with DiGraph core structure. Tests pass, WASM builds to 109KB (57KB gzipped).

title: Tutorial Model Infrastructure
description:
# Tutorial Model Infrastructure

## Background
The tutorial system needs a robust state machine to manage multi-page navigation, progress tracking, and integration with the main BubbleTea model. This is the foundation all other tutorial work builds upon.

## Technical Design

### TutorialModel struct
\`\`\`go
type TutorialModel struct {
    pages         []TutorialPage
    currentPage   int
    scrollOffset  int
    tocVisible    bool      // Table of contents sidebar
    progress      map[string]bool  // Sections viewed
    width, height int
    theme         Theme
    contextMode   bool      // true = context-specific help
    context       string    // Current view context (list, board, graph, etc.)
}

type TutorialPage struct {
    ID          string    // e.g., "intro", "navigation", "graph-view"
    Title       string
    Content     string    // Markdown content
    Section     string    // Parent section for TOC grouping
    Context     []string  // Which contexts this page applies to
}
\`\`\`

### Key Methods
- `Init() tea.Cmd` - Initialize tutorial
- `Update(msg tea.Msg) (TutorialModel, tea.Cmd)` - Handle navigation
- `View() string` - Render current page with chrome
- `NextPage()`, `PrevPage()` - Navigation
- `JumpToSection(id string)` - TOC navigation
- `SetContext(ctx string)` - Filter to context-relevant pages
- `MarkViewed(pageID string)` - Track progress

### Integration Points
- Main Model gets `showTutorial bool` and `tutorialModel TutorialModel`
- Tutorial is an overlay (like help), not a new view mode
- Can exit anytime with Escape

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] TutorialModel struct defined with all fields
- [ ] Basic page navigation (next/prev) works
- [ ] Scroll within long pages works
- [ ] Progress tracking persists to config
- [ ] Integrates with main Model as overlay
- [ ] Escape closes tutorial, returns to previous state

## Implementation Notes
- Use atomic.Value for thread-safe progress updates if needed
- Consider whether to pause file watcher during tutorial (probably not)
- Page content loaded lazily or all at once? All at once is fine for ~10 pages

## Estimated Complexity
Medium - This is foundational but well-understood patterns from existing overlays (help, label picker).

## Dependencies
None - this is the foundation.

title: Epic: Tree View Viewport Scrolling
description:
## Background & Motivation

The tree view (`pkg/ui/tree.go`) currently renders ALL visible nodes in the `View()` method. For typical usage (50-100 visible nodes), performance is acceptable:

- 50 nodes @ 80x24: ~1.1ms ✓
- 100 nodes @ 120x40: ~6.3ms ✓ (close to 5ms target)
- 200 nodes @ 160x50: ~31ms ⚠️ (edge case - rarely seen in practice)

**This epic is P3 (nice-to-have)** because current performance is acceptable for typical usage. Only pursue if users report actual slowness with large expanded trees.

## Key Insight: USE EXISTING BUBBLES VIEWPORT

The `TreeModel` already has an unused `viewport.Model` field:
```go
type TreeModel struct {
    viewport viewport.Model  // <-- EXISTS BUT UNUSED
    // ...
}
```

**Instead of reimplementing**, we should leverage `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/viewport` which handles:
- Content scrolling
- Cursor-follows-viewport
- Page up/down
- Keyboard bindings

This significantly reduces implementation effort.

## Approach

1. Feed rendered tree content to viewport.Model
2. Let viewport handle scrolling logic
3. Only implement custom logic if viewport doesn't meet needs

## Success Criteria

- [ ] BenchmarkTreeRender100 < 5ms (currently ~6.3ms - already close)
- [ ] Memory allocations reduced for large trees
- [ ] Smooth scrolling using bubbles viewport
- [ ] Cursor always visible

## When to Implement

- **Now**: If users report tree view slowness with 100+ visible nodes
- **Defer**: If no user complaints - current performance is acceptable

## Dependencies

None - tree view is stable (bv-gllx complete ✓)

## Labels

performance, tree-view, ui, nice-to-have
close_reason: All 5 child tasks completed. Performance targets exceeded: 100-node render improved from 6.3ms to 0.34ms (target was <5ms). 200-node render improved from 31ms to 0.47ms. Cursor-follows-viewport implemented.
